blocks.text: When a salt dissolves in water it dissociates into its constituent ions. These ions can interact with water, affecting the solution's pH depending on the nature of the acid and base from which the salt is derived. The four cases, salts of strong or weak acids with strong or weak bases, are treated in the next four topics.

blocks.title: Salt hydrolysis
blocks.text: Salt hydrolysis is the reaction of the ions of a dissolved salt with water, which makes the solution acidic, basic or neutral according to the strengths of the parent acid and base.

blocks.prompt: Why does dissolving some salts change the pH of water while dissolving others does not?
blocks.explanation: A dissolved ion changes the pH only if it reacts with water: the conjugate base of a weak acid takes protons from water and releases OH-, and the conjugate acid of a weak base gives protons to water and forms H3O+. Ions derived from strong acids or strong bases are such weak conjugates that they do not react, so the solution stays neutral.

items: Salt ions can react with water (hydrolyse) and shift the pH; the outcome depends on whether the parent acid and base were strong or weak.
